follow_up_reason: Two-week follow-up after trouble sleeping due to work stress

clinician_brief.prior_note: Two weeks ago, Daniel reported difficulty falling asleep and feeling stressed because of a demanding project at work. There were no symptoms of a depressive or anxiety disorder, and he did not want to start any medicine. He was advised to improve his sleep habits (regular bedtime, less screen time at night, less caffeine after midday) and to try simple stress-relief activities.
active_problems: Situational stress and mild insomnia (no medicine started)
previous_plan: Keep a regular sleep and wake time
Try short walks or relaxation exercises to manage stress
Return in two weeks if not improved
results_and_observations: No tests were needed at the first visit
today_tasks: Ask how his sleep has been since the last visit
Ask about his stress levels and the work project
Check which changes he tried and how they helped
Screen for symptoms of depression or anxiety

patient_private.interval_history: Falling asleep faster most nights; still has one or two rough nights when work is very busy.
patient_private.adherence: Started going to bed at the same time and cut back on his phone use at night; still drinks coffee in the afternoon sometimes.
patient_private.treatment_response: Feels more rested overall and less irritable during the day.
patient_private.side_effects: Not applicable — no medicine was started.
patient_private.new_symptoms_and_red_flags: No low mood most of the day, no loss of interest in things he enjoys, no thoughts of harming himself.
patient_private.agenda: Wants to know if his sleep is good enough now or if he needs anything else.
patient_private.concern: Worried the stress will come back once a new project starts next month.
patient_private.preference: Would rather keep managing this with lifestyle changes than start any medicine.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Two-week review of situational insomnia and work stress managed with sleep-hygiene changes, no medication
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: Situational insomnia tied to a clear stressor (a demanding work project) often responds well to first-line behavioral measures — consistent sleep/wake times, reduced evening screen exposure, and limiting afternoon caffeine — without needing medication, which matches Daniel's improvement.

Improvement doesn't need to be perfect to be a success: falling asleep faster on most nights with occasional rough nights during high-stress periods is a realistic, expected pattern of partial but meaningful progress.

A brief screen for low mood, anhedonia, and safety (thoughts of self-harm) is a standard part of any insomnia or stress follow-up, since sleep disturbance and depression/anxiety commonly overlap and either can be the primary driver.

Anticipating a future stressor (the new project next month) is an opportunity for proactive planning — reinforcing which behavioral tools worked so he can redeploy them early, rather than waiting for symptoms to return.
diagnostic_clues: Falling asleep faster on most nights, with occasional rough nights only when work is very busy, shows a clear link between the stressor and residual symptoms rather than a fixed sleep disorder.

Consistent bedtime and reduced night-time phone use were adopted, while afternoon caffeine intake persists — an incomplete but meaningful adherence pattern worth exploring rather than assuming full compliance or none at all.
Feeling more rested and less irritable during the day is an objective marker that the sleep changes are translating into real functional improvement, not just subjective optimism.

No low mood most of the day, no loss of interest in enjoyable activities, and no thoughts of self-harm are reassuring negatives that argue against an evolving depressive or anxiety disorder underlying the sleep complaint.
common_misconceptions: Worried the stress will come back once a new project starts next month — a realistic concern; addressing it now by naming which strategies worked (regular bedtime, less screen time) gives him a plan to use proactively rather than waiting to react.

Would rather keep managing this with lifestyle changes than start any medicine — a reasonable preference to honor, since his current partial response with behavioral measures alone suggests medication is not yet indicated.

Wants to know if his sleep is good enough now or if he needs anything else — patients sometimes think 'good enough' is binary, when in practice a still-improving trend with an identifiable trigger (workload) is a positive sign that doesn't necessarily require any escalation.

Assuming afternoon caffeine has no effect on nighttime sleep since he doesn't feel 'wired,' when caffeine's half-life means an early-afternoon dose can still be affecting sleep onset many hours later.
dangerous_errors: Not screening for depression or anxiety symptoms before attributing ongoing rough nights entirely to work stress, since insomnia is also a common presenting symptom of a mood or anxiety disorder.
Failing to ask directly about thoughts of self-harm as part of the safety screen, even when the visit otherwise seems reassuring.
Assuming afternoon caffeine intake is irrelevant to his residual symptoms rather than identifying it as an easily modifiable remaining factor.
Offering to start a sleep medication reflexively when he has already shown a good behavioral response and has explicitly stated a preference to avoid medication.
management_principles: Confirm the improved sleep and mood trajectory and connect it explicitly to the specific changes he made (regular bedtime, less screen time).
Complete a brief depression/anxiety and self-harm safety screen before concluding stress alone explains any residual symptoms.
Address the one incomplete behavioral change — afternoon caffeine — as a concrete, low-effort next step rather than introducing medication.
Proactively plan for the anticipated stress of the new project, reinforcing which specific strategies to restart early rather than waiting for sleep to worsen again.
boundaries_and_exceptions: If low mood, loss of interest, or persistent daytime dysfunction develop or worsen, this lifestyle-focused plan no longer applies and evaluation for a primary mood or anxiety disorder is warranted.

If insomnia persists most nights beyond several weeks despite consistent behavioral measures, this would meet a threshold to consider referral for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) rather than continuing lifestyle advice alone.
